source.text: Wonhyo, Arouse Your Mind and Practice: the second part of the Admonitions for Beginners (Chobalsim Jagyeongmun)
source.translationLicense: English translation and commentary: newly made by Sutra Box from its own Korean version (based on an AI draft, still being reviewed and refined)

w01.heading: Buddhas and Beings
w01.plain: All the Buddhas adorn the tranquil palace of nirvana because for countless ages they gave up desire and practiced austerities. Beings keep circling at the gate of the burning house because for measureless ages they could not let go of craving.
w01.commentary: Master Wonhyo wrote this to urge monastics to arouse the resolve to practice. He begins by saying that the difference between Buddhas and beings lies in whether they have let go of desire.

w02.heading: Heaven No One Bars, Evil Paths No One Lures
w02.plain: No one bars the way to heaven, yet few go there, because they treat the afflictions of the three poisons as their household wealth. No one lures them to the evil paths, yet many go in, because they treat the body and the five desires as treasures of a deluded mind. Who does not want to go into the mountains and cultivate the Way? They cannot go forward because they are bound by attachment.
w02.commentary: "The four snakes" likens the four elements that make up the body (earth, water, fire and wind) to poisonous snakes.

w03.heading: Do Good as Far as You Can
w03.plain: Even if you cannot go into the mountains to cultivate the mind, do not give up good deeds as far as your strength allows. If you can give up your own pleasure, you will be trusted and revered like a sage; if you can do what is hard to do, you will be honored like a Buddha. Stinginess and greed for things make you one of Māra's retinue; compassionate giving makes you a child of the Dharma King.
w03.commentary: This opens a path even for those who cannot leave home, which is why lay people can read this text too.

w04.heading: Life in the Mountains
w04.plain: High peaks and steep rocks are where the wise live; green pines and deep valleys are where practitioners dwell. When hungry, ease the empty stomach with fruit from the trees; when thirsty, quench the thirst with running water. Feed this body sweets and cherish it, and still it will surely break down; dress it in soft clothes and guard it, and still life will surely end.

w05.heading: Let the Echoing Cave Be Your Hall
w05.plain: Make the echoing cave in the rock your hall for reciting the Buddha's name, and make the mournful birds your heart's companions. Even if your knees grow cold as ice from bowing, do not long for a fire; even if your empty stomach aches as if cut, do not think of seeking food. A hundred years pass in a moment; how can you not learn? How long is one lifetime; how can you idle it away without practice?
w05.commentary: "A hundred years pass in a moment; how can you not learn? How long is one lifetime; how can you not practice?" is one of the most quoted lines of this text.

w06.heading: Monastics and Leaving Home
w06.plain: One who has let go of attachment in the heart is called a śramaṇa; one who does not long for the world is said to have left home. A practitioner in silk clothes is like a dog wearing an elephant's hide; a person of the Way who harbors longing is like a hedgehog crawling into a mouse hole. Though talented and wise, one who lives in town makes the Buddhas grieve; though lacking in practice, one who stays in the mountains makes the sages rejoice.

w07.heading: Precepts and Wisdom
w07.plain: Talent and learning without keeping the precepts are like being guided to a treasure and never setting out. Diligent practice without wisdom is like wanting to go east while walking west. The practice of the wise is like steaming rice to make a meal; the practice of the unwise is like steaming sand to make a meal. Everyone knows to eat to ease an empty stomach, yet no one knows to learn the Dharma to mend a foolish mind. Practice and wisdom together are like the two wheels of a cart; benefiting oneself and others is like the two wings of a bird.
w07.commentary: The image of "steaming sand to make rice" warns against practice without wisdom.

w08.heading: The Shame of Receiving Offerings
w08.plain: If you receive porridge and chant a blessing without understanding its meaning, should you not feel ashamed before the donor? If you receive a meal and chant verses without grasping their meaning, should you not feel ashamed before the sages? As people loathe worms that do not tell clean from foul, so the sages despise a monastic who does not tell pure from impure.
w08.commentary: The donor is a lay supporter who makes offerings. This is a reminder of how weighty it is to receive offerings.

w09.heading: The Precepts Are a Good Ladder
w09.plain: To leave the world's clamor and rise to the heavens, the precepts are a good ladder. So to break the precepts and still try to be a field of merit for others is like a bird with broken wings trying to fly carrying a turtle on its back. If you cannot free yourself from your own wrongs, you cannot redeem the wrongs of others. How then can you accept others' offerings without keeping the precepts? Feeding an empty body without practice brings no benefit; cherishing this fleeting, impermanent life cannot preserve it.

w10.heading: Practice Now
w10.plain: If you hope for the great virtue of dragons and elephants, endure long hardship; if you aim for the lion's seat, turn your back on pleasure forever. When a practitioner's mind is pure, all the gods praise them together; when a person of the Way longs for sensual things, the good spirits leave. The body suddenly scatters and cannot stay long. It is already evening today; should you not have practiced from the morning? Worldly pleasure turns into suffering later; why cling to it? One moment of patience brings lasting joy; why not practice? Greed in a person of the Way is a practitioner's shame; wealth in one who has left home is a laughingstock to the noble.

w11.heading: Endless Excuses
w11.plain: Excuses never end, so clinging never stops. Putting things off never ends, so attachment is never cut. One affair after another without limit, so worldly business is never given up. One scheme after another without end, so the resolve to cut it off never arises. Putting it off today, the days of doing harm grow many; putting it off tomorrow, the days of doing good grow few. Putting it off this year, afflictions are endless; putting it off next year, one never advances toward awakening.
w11.commentary: A sharp look at the mind that puts off practice. The phrase "putting things off never ends" follows the standard edition used in Korean monastic seminaries; other editions give slightly different characters.

w12.heading: Hurry, Hurry
w12.plain: Hours pass and pass, and suddenly a day is gone; days pass and pass, and suddenly the month has ended; months pass and pass, and all at once a year arrives; years pass and pass, and in a moment you reach the gate of death. A broken cart cannot move; an old person cannot practice. Lying down, laziness arises; sitting up, thoughts are scattered. How many lives have you spent without practice, wasting days and nights? How many times have you lived an empty life? If you do not practice in this life either, this body will surely end; what then of the next? Should you not hurry? Should you not hurry?
w12.commentary: It ends by repeating "Should you not hurry?" twice: a heartfelt plea to arouse the mind right now, since time never stops flowing.
